37772:
Jude is only twenty-five verses long, but it is carefully crafted. Richard Bauckham has shown that its central section is a piece of Jewish interpretation: it states a theme, gives examples from Scripture and tradition, then applies each with 'these people are...', much like the commentaries (pesharim) found among the Dead Sea Scrolls.

Jude draws freely on Jewish traditions beyond the Hebrew Bible. Verse 6, about angels who left their proper home and are kept in chains for judgment, reflects the story of the Watchers in 1 Enoch. Verse 9, about the archangel Michael disputing with the devil over Moses' body, comes, according to Clement of Alexandria and Origen, from a work called the Assumption (or Testament) of Moses, whose ending is lost. Verses 14-15 quote 1 Enoch 1:9 almost word for word, introducing it as something Enoch 'prophesied'. 1 Enoch was widely read in the Second Temple period; fragments of it were found at Qumran, and it remains part of the Ethiopian Orthodox canon.

Because of these citations some early Christians hesitated over Jude, and Jerome mentions that many rejected it for this reason. Yet it is listed in the Muratorian fragment and was accepted by Tertullian, Clement and Origen, and it entered all the major canon lists.
37774: 1 Enoch is a collection of Jewish apocalyptic writings (third century BC onward) about Enoch, the fallen Watchers and final judgment. Jude quotes it as genuine prophecy, showing that his community valued it.
37776: Early believers shared common meals (agapai) that included the Lord's Supper. The intruders are 'hidden reefs' at these meals, dangerous because unseen, and shepherds feeding only themselves.
37778: Even Michael, the great archangel, did not dare insult the devil but said 'The Lord rebuke you', echoing Zechariah. The intruders, by contrast, 'blaspheme glorious ones'.
37780: Jewish teaching often grouped stock examples of rebellion and judgment. Jude's triads (wilderness Israel, Watchers, Sodom; Cain, Balaam, Korah) come from this tradition.
37781: Jewish prayers ended with blessing God for glory and majesty forever. Jude's closing doxology, one of the most loved in Scripture, gives the same praise 'through Jesus Christ our Lord'.
37782:
Jude is perhaps the most thoroughly Jewish document in the New Testament, a window into the faith of Jesus' own family. Its examples come from Israel's story (the exodus generation, Sodom, Cain, Balaam, Korah) and from the wider Jewish tradition of Enoch and Moses. Its way of arguing, matching ancient types to present people, is the method of Jewish apocalyptic interpretation. Its hope is Enoch's: the Lord coming with his holy ones to judge the ungodly.

For a Jewish-rooted audience, Jude's message is covenantal. God saved a people out of Egypt but later judged those in that very generation who did not trust him, so grace is not a licence to rebel. Yet the letter is bracketed by assurance: the readers are 'called, beloved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ', and God 'is able to keep you from stumbling'. Their part is to build themselves up in faith, pray in the Spirit and keep themselves in God's love while waiting for mercy, and to snatch others from the fire. It is the call to covenant loyalty that runs from Deuteronomy through the prophets.
37784: Jude greets believers loved by God and kept for Jesus Christ.
37786: Intruders have slipped in, turning grace into licence and denying the Master.
37788: The exodus generation, the Watchers and Sodom show that God judges rebellion.
37790: The intruders reject authority, follow Cain, Balaam and Korah, and are barren clouds and wandering stars.
37792: Enoch and the apostles warned of the Lord's judgment on scoffers.
37794: Build up, pray, wait for mercy, and show mercy to the doubting and endangered.
37796: God is able to keep them from stumbling and present them blameless with joy.
37797: Contend for the faith, kept by God
37821: To struggle earnestly, like an athlete, for the faith handed down.
37823: Key word: believers are kept by God, keep themselves in his love, while rebels are kept for judgment.
37825: Unrestrained sensuality, throwing off moral limits.
37827: God's covenant compassion (Hebrew hesed), received and shown.
37828: 2 Peter reuses much of Jude's material, generally removing the explicit non-canonical references.
37829: Enoch, the sons of God, Sodom and Cain all come from Genesis.
37830: Balaam and Korah's rebellion and the wilderness judgments.
37831: 'The Lord rebuke you' echoes the angel's word to Satan.
37832: Written by brothers of Jesus, both letters share a strongly Jewish-Christian outlook.
37833: Jude calls Jesus 'our only Master and Lord', and some of the best manuscripts of verse 5 even say that Jesus saved the people out of Egypt, placing him in Israel's story as the LORD. The letter shows how quickly Jesus' own Jewish family came to worship him within the framework of Jewish monotheism.
37834: Jude's use of 1 Enoch: either Enoch is Scripture or Jude made a mistake
37835: Readers who discover that Jude quotes 1 Enoch often feel forced to choose: either 1 Enoch should be in the Bible, or Jude's inspiration is compromised.
37836: Richard Bauckham and Gene Green show that Jude, like other Jews of his time, valued 1 Enoch as containing true prophecy without thereby making it part of a fixed canon (which was still settling). Paul quotes Greek poets without endorsing everything they wrote. Jude's community knew and loved these traditions, so he argues from what they already accepted.
37837: Conservative scholars such as Thomas Schreiner and Douglas Moo say that Jude affirms the truth of the specific prophecy he quotes, not the inspiration of the whole book. Some Ethiopian Orthodox Christians, who include 1 Enoch in their canon, see Jude as support for that. Scholars agree that Jude's practice shows how broad the early Jewish reading world was.
37838: Knowing Jude's sources helps readers understand the Jewish world of the New Testament without fear that it undermines Scripture.
37839: 'Contend for the faith' means fighting culture wars
37840: Jude 3 is often used as a slogan for aggressive defence of doctrine or for political and cultural battles against outsiders.
37841: Jude's opponents are inside the community, at its love feasts, and the issue is moral as much as doctrinal: using grace as an excuse for immorality. The letter's response is not attack but building up in faith, prayer, staying in God's love and showing mercy, even snatching people from the fire. Bauckham notes that the positive instruction in verses 20-23 is the letter's real goal.
37842: Evangelical scholars rightly stress that Jude does call for firm defence of apostolic teaching and that some teaching must be resisted. They agree that the manner Jude commends includes mercy and humility, as with Michael's restraint.
37843: Read whole, Jude teaches believers to stand firm without becoming harsh, keeping mercy alongside conviction.
37844: A community infiltrated by smooth-talking teachers was told that grace is not licence, that God judges rebellion, and that he keeps those who keep themselves in his love.
37845: Jude warns against using grace as cover for self-indulgence and against leaders who serve themselves, while calling believers to prayer, mercy and joyful confidence in God's power to keep them.
37846: A prophetic vision given to seven real churches in Roman Asia, unveiling that the slain Lamb, not Caesar, rules history, and calling them to faithful witness until God makes all things new.
37847: John, a prophet exiled on Patmos
37848: A Jewish-Christian prophet named John, well known to the seven churches, who was on Patmos 'because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus' and who thinks in Hebrew while writing in rough, Semitic Greek.
37849: He names himself four times but never claims to be an apostle. Justin Martyr and Irenaeus identified him with the apostle John. Dionysius of Alexandria in the third century argued from style that he was a different John, and most modern scholars agree; a minority defends the apostle.
37850: John's Gospel and letters (traditionally; most scholars think a different author)
37851: Patmos, a small island in the Aegean
37852: John says he was on Patmos when he received the vision. The book may have been written there or shortly after on the mainland.
37853: Seven churches in the Roman province of Asia: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, Laodicea
37855: Some churches faced slander, imprisonment and even death (Antipas at Pergamum); others were comfortable, wealthy and compromising with trade-guild feasts and civic religion. Most scholars date the book to Domitian's reign (c. 95), following Irenaeus; some argue for the late 60s after Nero. Recent research (Leonard Thompson, Steven Friesen) suggests the pressure came less from an empire-wide persecution than from local imperial cult and social life, which John saw as a deeper danger.
37856: Pergamum receives permission for a temple to Roma and Augustus, the first in Asia.
37857: Smyrna wins the right to build a temple to Tiberius (Tacitus, Annals 4.55-56).
37858: Earthquake hits Laodicea, which rebuilds from its own wealth without imperial aid (Tacitus, Annals 14.27).
37859: Nero's persecution of Christians in Rome; Nero dies in 68, and legends arise that he would return.
37860: Temple in Jerusalem destroyed by Titus.
37861: Temple of the Sebastoi (the Flavian emperors) dedicated at Ephesus (c. 89-90).
37862:
Revelation combines three genres. It is an apocalypse, a Jewish literary form (like Daniel 7-12 or 1 Enoch) in which a seer is shown heavenly realities through symbols, angels and numbers. It is a prophecy, a message from God calling hearers to respond now. And it is a letter, addressed to seven real churches, meant to be read aloud in worship: 'blessed is the one who reads aloud and those who hear'.

The province of Asia was proud and prosperous, and it competed for the honour of building temples to the emperors. Pergamum hosted the first temple to Roma and Augustus; Smyrna built one for Tiberius; Ephesus dedicated a great temple to the Flavian emperors around 89-90. Emperor worship was woven into festivals, trade-guild banquets, coinage and civic identity. Refusing to take part could mean losing business and friends, or worse. Domitian reportedly liked to be addressed as 'lord and god', though historians debate how far that reflects his own policy. Meanwhile, the Jewish communities in Asia had legal privileges, and tension between some synagogues and Jesus-followers appears in the letters to Smyrna and Philadelphia.

John's visions expose this world. Rome is the beast from the sea, sitting on seven hills; its prophets of the imperial cult are the beast from the land; and the city is 'Babylon the great', the luxurious prostitute whose trade in goods and 'human souls' enriches merchants. The number 666 most likely spells 'Nero Caesar' in Hebrew letters, which also explains the ancient variant 616.
37864: Temples, priests, sacrifices and festivals honoured the emperors as divine or semi-divine. For the cities it expressed loyalty and gratitude; for John it was idolatry. The beasts, the mark and the worship of the image use this world.
37866: Guild meetings involved meals honouring patron gods. 'Balaam' and 'Jezebel' at Pergamum and Thyatira seem to have taught that eating idol food was acceptable, a way to keep business and status.
37868: Laodicea was a rich banking, textile and medical centre. Babylon's cargo list of luxury goods ends with 'slaves, that is, human souls', exposing the economics of empire.
37870: In Hebrew and Greek, letters doubled as numbers. Seven means completeness, twelve the people of God, and 666 most likely spells 'Neron Kaisar' in Hebrew letters.
37872: In Smyrna and Philadelphia, John calls some opponents 'a synagogue of Satan' who 'say they are Jews and are not'. This is an intra-Jewish dispute over who are God's true people, written by a Jew, not a statement about Jews in general.
37873: Lampstands, incense, altar, white robes, harps and hymns all come from the Jerusalem temple. Heaven is pictured as the true sanctuary, and the new Jerusalem is a cube like the most holy place.
37874:
Revelation is the most Jewish book in the New Testament in its imagery. It has more allusions to the Hebrew Scriptures than any other New Testament book, though it never formally quotes them: the throne-chariot of Ezekiel, the beasts and Son of Man of Daniel, the plagues of Exodus, the lampstands of Zechariah, the fall of Babylon in Jeremiah and Isaiah, and the new Jerusalem of Ezekiel 40-48 and Isaiah 65. Its genre, the apocalypse, is a Jewish form born in times of imperial oppression, from Daniel under the Greeks to 4 Ezra and 2 Baruch, written after Rome destroyed the temple. A first-century Jew would hear Rome as the latest Babylon and the beast as the fourth beast of Daniel.

The central vision turns the story on its head. John hears of 'the Lion of the tribe of Judah', the Davidic warrior Messiah, but when he turns he sees a Lamb standing as though slain. Victory comes by sacrificial faithfulness, the way of Isaiah's servant and the Passover lamb. The redeemed are counted as the twelve tribes of Israel (144,000) and then seen as a countless multitude from every nation: a single people of God in which the nations join Israel's worship. The ending is Israel's hope fulfilled: not escape from earth but God's dwelling (the shekinah, the tabernacle presence) coming down to live with his people, the river and tree of life of Eden and Ezekiel restored, and the leaves of the tree 'for the healing of the nations'.
37876: John on Patmos sees the Son of Man among seven lampstands, holding the churches.
37878: Each church is praised, warned and promised rewards for 'conquering' through faithfulness.
37880: Heaven's worship centres on God the Creator and the slain Lamb who is worthy to open the scroll.
37882: Cycles of judgment echo the exodus plagues, while God's people are sealed and bear witness.
37884: The cosmic conflict behind Rome: the dragon, the beast from the sea and the beast from the land.
37886: Bowls of wrath and the fall of the great city expose empire's violence and luxury.
37888: The rider called the Word of God defeats the beast; Satan is bound and finally judged.
37890: New heavens and earth; God dwells with his people in the new Jerusalem.
37891: The Lamb who was slain reigns
37912: An uncovering of what is hidden: the true state of the world from heaven's view.
37914: Faithful testimony to Jesus, often costing life; Jesus is the faithful witness.
37916: To win the victory; in Revelation, by faithful suffering like the Lamb, not by violence.
37918: Jesus' main title in Revelation (twenty-eight times): the slain yet living Passover lamb.
37920: Beasts, the Son of Man, sealed books and time periods all come from Daniel.
37921: The throne-chariot, eating the scroll, Gog and Magog and the river of life from the city echo Ezekiel.
37922: Plagues, the song of Moses and the kingdom of priests shape the story of a new exodus.
37923: New heavens and new earth, no more tears, and the fall of Babylon.
37924: The tree of life, river and the end of the curse bring Eden's story full circle.
37925: 'Come out of her, my people' echoes the call to flee Babylon.
37926: Jesus is the faithful witness, firstborn from the dead and ruler of the kings of the earth, the Son of Man, the Lion who is the Lamb, and the Alpha and Omega who shares God's throne and receives the same worship. Jewish readers recognise the apocalyptic form and imagery; Christians see in the slain Lamb the heart of the book: God's victory through self-giving love.
37927: Revelation is a coded guide to today's headlines
37928: Many popular books and preachers read Revelation as a detailed prediction of modern events, matching beasts, plagues and the mark with current nations, technologies and leaders.
37929: Revelation was written to seven real churches and had to make sense to them ('the time is near'). Its symbols draw on the Hebrew Scriptures and on Roman realities: seven hills, imperial worship, Nero. Richard Bauckham, Michael Gorman and Craig Koester read it as prophetic unveiling of empire in every age, not as a timetable for ours. Each generation that matched it to its own headlines has been wrong in the details.
37930: Futurist interpreters, including dispensational scholars (for example Robert Thomas) and historic premillennialists, argue that much of Revelation does describe future events before Christ's return, though careful futurists also warn against date-setting and headline matching. Preterist, historicist, idealist and futurist approaches remain a real scholarly debate; many scholars combine them.
37931: Treating Revelation as a decoder breeds fear and speculation. Reading it in its setting calls believers to worship, endurance and faithful resistance to idolatry now.
37932: Revelation teaches a secret rapture before the tribulation
37933: Dispensational teaching often reads the voice saying 'come up here' to John as a picture of the church being raptured, so the church is absent from the earth during the judgments of chapters 6-19.
37934: In its setting, 'come up here' is John's personal call into the heavenly throne room, like the prophets' visions. God's servants are present on earth throughout, sealed and protected through suffering, not removed from it. Barbara Rossing, Craig Keener and Michael Gorman note that Revelation's call is to endure and witness, and that its future hope is God coming down to dwell on earth.
37935: Pre-tribulation scholars (for example John Walvoord and Robert Thomas) argue that the word 'church' disappears after chapter 3 and that promises of being kept 'from the hour of trial' imply removal, combining Revelation with 1 Thessalonians 4. Many other evangelicals (historic premillennialists like George Ladd, amillennialists like G. K. Beale) disagree. This is a real, ongoing debate within evangelicalism.
37936: Expecting to escape suffering can leave believers unprepared for it; Revelation prepares them to remain faithful in it.
37937: 'Synagogue of Satan' means Jews are Satan's people
37938: Some readers, and historically some anti-Jewish preachers, took Revelation 2:9 and 3:9 as a condemnation of Jews and Judaism as such.
37939: John is himself a Jew whose book honours the twelve tribes and the new Jerusalem. His words concern local opponents in two cities who, he believed, were denouncing Jesus-followers to authorities. 'Say they are Jews and are not' is a claim about who are true Jews, the kind of insider polemic found in the prophets and at Qumran. The Jewish Annotated New Testament and David Frankfurter discuss the passage in this light.
37940: Evangelical commentators such as G. K. Beale and Craig Keener agree it is not a statement about all Jews and reject any antisemitic use, while some read it as teaching that the church is now the true Israel. Whether John means Gentile believers or Jewish believers as 'true Jews' is debated.
37941: Correct reading prevents a polemical phrase from being turned into hatred of Jewish people, and reminds readers that John's quarrel was within Israel's family.
37942: For small churches in a powerful empire, Revelation unveiled that Caesar was not lord, that their faithful witness shared in the Lamb's victory, and that comfortable compromise was more dangerous than persecution.
37943: Revelation calls readers to worship God alone, to see through the idolatries of power and wealth in any age, to endure with hope, and to long for God's renewal of the earth, rather than to speculate about dates.
37944: Paul introduces his gospel to a divided church he has never met, showing that the God of Israel has kept his promises in the Messiah and now makes Jews and Gentiles one family that must welcome each other.
37946: A Jew of the tribe of Benjamin, trained as a Pharisee, who after meeting the risen Jesus saw himself as Israel's Messiah's envoy to the nations. By the time of Romans he had spent about twenty years planting churches from Syria to the Adriatic coast.
37947: The letter names Paul as sender (Rom 1:1) and Tertius as the man who physically wrote it (Rom 16:22). Its style, themes and travel plans match Galatians and the Corinthian letters, and no serious scholar doubts it. It was used by Clement of Rome in the 90s and was in every early collection of Paul's letters.
37949: Paul is about to take the money collected from Greek churches to Jerusalem (Rom 15:25-26). He commends Phoebe of Cenchreae, Corinth's eastern port, who probably carried the letter (Rom 16:1-2), and he is staying with Gaius (Rom 16:23), likely the Gaius he baptised in Corinth (1 Cor 1:14). This fits the three-month stay in Greece of Acts 20:2-3.
37950: Several house churches in Rome, a mixed body of Jewish and Gentile believers, with Gentiles probably the majority by now
37951: Paul had not founded or visited these churches. Romans 16 greets around 26 people and at least three household gatherings, so the 'church in Rome' was a network rather than one building. Jewish believers who had been expelled under Claudius had returned, and disputes about food and holy days were straining relationships between groups (Rom 14:1-6). Paul also needed Rome as a base and supporter for a new mission to Spain (Rom 15:24).
37953: Claudius expels Jews (or some Jews) from Rome after disturbances 'at the instigation of Chrestus', as Suetonius puts it; Priscilla and Aquila leave for Corinth (Acts 18:2). The year comes from the later writer Orosius and is debated.
37954: Claudius dies and Nero becomes emperor; the expulsion lapses and Jews, including Jewish believers, return to Rome.
37955: Paul writes Romans from Corinth before sailing for Jerusalem with the collection.
37956: Public complaints in Rome about abusive indirect taxes, recorded by Tacitus, Annals 13.50-51; some link this to Paul's advice on paying taxes and dues (Rom 13:6-7).
37957: Great Fire of Rome; Nero blames and executes Christians, some of whom may have heard this letter read.
